title: Rosemary
subtitle: The circulatory herb: infusions, infused oils, and baths for poor circulation and tired muscles
excerpt: Rosemary is the strongly aromatic kitchen shrub whose leaves and flowering tops have a long western herbal use for poor circulation, cold hands and feet, and tired muscles. The leaves are prepared as a hot infusion, an infused oil for massage, or a bath for the whole body. Fresh rosemary from the garden or a jar of dried leaf keeps preparation available year-round.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb or preparation applied to the skin that causes local warming and redness by drawing blood to the area, traditionally used for muscle pain and poor local circulation.
A herb traditionally used to encourage blood flow, often experienced as a warming sensation in the hands, feet, or the area of application.

content.text: Salvia rosmarinus Spenn. (synonym: Rosmarinus officinalis L.), family Lamiaceae. An aromatic evergreen shrub, 0.5,2 m, with needle-like grey-green leaves, silver-white underneath, and small blue-violet flowers from late winter through spring. Native to the Mediterranean coast. widely grown as a culinary and garden plant across temperate Europe. The leaves and flowering tops are used fresh or dried. Harvest before or at flowering.

The leaf carries a rich volatile oil (camphor, borneol, cineole) along with rosmarinic acid, flavonoids, and diterpene compounds. The volatile oil supports the warming circulatory action the herb is known for. Camphor gives the stimulating character. Borneol contributes to the muscle-easing element.

The herbalist Culpeper used rosemary for cold aches and head complaints. The herbalist Grieve noted its use for poor-circulation headaches and as a hair rinse. Current guidance supports rosemary leaf for mild muscle spasm and circulation support. It is also used as a skin rinse.

Hot infusion: 1 teaspoon of dried rosemary leaf (or 2 to 3 sprigs of fresh) per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 8 minutes. One to two cups daily. Do not drink more than 2 cups a day. rosemary in large doses can be overstimulating.

Infused oil: 1 part dried rosemary to 5 parts olive oil by weight. Double boiler at 60 to 65°C for 2 to 4 hours, then strain. Use as a warm massage oil for tired or aching muscles. Keeps 12 months in a dark bottle.

Bath: 50 to 100 g dried rosemary leaf steeped in 1 litre of just-boiled water for 20 minutes, strained, added to a warm bath. Invigorating and warming. best in the morning or early afternoon rather than at bedtime.
Pregnancy: culinary quantities are safe. For regular medicinal use, consult a herbalist or midwife first.
Hypertension: rosemary may raise blood pressure. If you have high blood pressure or take blood-pressure medication, discuss medicinal rosemary use with your prescriber first.
Epilepsy: rosemary contains camphor. Camphor excites the nervous system. Avoid medicinal doses if you have epilepsy or take epilepsy drugs.
